title: The Plateau

scenario.situation: A UX improvement to the onboarding flow showed no statistically significant lift on the overall activation metric in an A/B test. The team is ready to scrap the change.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team concludes the redesign simply didn't work — the activation rate was nearly identical between control and treatment — and plans to move on to a different experiment.
scenario.question: Did the UX change actually fail, or is something in the data structure hiding a real effect?

decisions.prompt: The team says the test failed and wants to move on. How do you frame your investigation before agreeing?

options.label: Recheck statistical significance
options.detail: Run the significance test again with a longer observation window to make sure the null result is real.
options.consequence: You extend the window and confirm: still no significant lift overall. You've validated the null result but never questioned whether the aggregate metric is the right lens. The real signal remains invisible.
options.divergenceCost: Doubled down on the aggregate view instead of questioning whether it could even detect an effect.

options.label: Diagnostic segmentation by baseline activation
options.detail: Before accepting the null result, segment users by their pre-test activation baseline to check whether headroom varies across groups.
options.consequence: Immediately you see the population splits into two very different groups: one already activating near 100%, the other with substantial room to grow. The aggregate metric was averaging across incompatible situations — the investigation is now pointed at the right question.

options.label: Interview users who didn't activate
options.detail: Talk to non-activators in both arms to understand qualitative blockers.
options.consequence: Interviews surface general friction themes but can't explain why the aggregate metric showed no lift. You've gathered useful color without diagnosing the structural issue in the test design.
options.divergenceCost: Reached for qualitative research before exhausting what the existing data could reveal.

options.label: Test a different UX variant instead
options.detail: Accept the null result and immediately design a follow-up experiment with a bolder change.
options.consequence: A new experiment starts, but it's aimed at the same high-baseline segment. You've iterated without diagnosing — the ceiling effect will likely suppress the new result too.
options.divergenceCost: Iterated on the solution before understanding why the measurement failed.

decisions.prompt: You've split users by baseline activation level. Which metric view do you use to evaluate the experiment's true effect?

artifact.title: Activation rate — Treatment vs Control (overall)
artifact.caption: Overall activation rates look nearly identical. The 0.6pp difference is well within noise — but this collapses two very different user groups into one number.

options.label: Overall activation rate (treatment vs. control)
options.detail: Compare the single aggregate activation rate between arms.
options.consequence: The rates are 91.2% vs 91.8% — indistinguishable. You confirm the null result and move on, never realizing you were averaging a ceiling-constrained group with a headroom-rich group, which mathematically guaranteed a near-zero aggregate lift.
options.divergenceCost: Trusted an aggregate metric that structurally could not surface a segment-level effect.

options.label: Activation rate by segment — high-baseline vs. low-baseline
options.detail: Split treatment and control within each baseline segment and compare rates separately.
options.consequence: The segmented view is unambiguous: in the high-baseline segment both arms sit at ~96%, confirming no headroom for any intervention to show lift. In the low-baseline segment, treatment activates at 71% vs. control's 58% — a 13pp lift. The UX change works; it was just invisible in the aggregate.

artifact.title: Activation rate by segment — Treatment vs Control
artifact.caption: Segmented by baseline headroom, the low-baseline treatment arm lifts 13pp — a real, material effect that the aggregate metric completely buried.

decisions.prompt: The segmented data shows a 13pp lift in the low-baseline group and near-zero movement in the high-baseline group. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "The change works — ship it to low-baseline users immediately."
options.detail: Declare the segmented lift causal and recommend a targeted rollout now.
options.consequence: You act on a post-hoc subgroup finding without confirming it in a pre-specified test. The segment split wasn't planned before the experiment, so the 13pp lift could partially reflect multiple-comparison noise or a confounded segment definition — you've overclaimed a correlational pattern as established fact.
options.divergenceCost: Treated a post-hoc subgroup finding as a confirmed causal result without a pre-registered replication.

options.label: "The aggregate null result was a ceiling artifact; the low-baseline segment shows a strong correlate of lift — we should pre-register a targeted retest in that segment before shipping."
options.detail: Present the finding as a hypothesis generated by the data, not a proven conclusion, and propose a confirmatory experiment.
options.consequence: The team sees both the evidence and its limits: the redesign is almost certainly helping users who had room to improve, but the finding was found post-hoc and deserves a clean confirmatory test. You've rescued a valuable change from the scrap pile AND maintained analytical credibility.

insight: The UX change wasn't a failure — the measurement was. When ~96% of the tested segment was already activating, the aggregate metric had almost no mathematical room to move, guaranteeing a near-zero result regardless of whether the change worked. Segmenting by baseline headroom revealed a genuine 13pp lift in users who actually needed help. The lesson: before concluding an intervention has no effect, ask whether the metric could have detected one — ceiling effects routinely bury real signals in aggregate numbers.
